title: AlphaDestiny Novice Program review (part. 1: training)
summary: NH reviews the training side of AlphaDestiny's 2-day full-body novice program. He praises its evolving set/rep scheme (3-5 sets of 4-6 reps) and inclusion of isolation work, but would swap box squats for free squats, floor press for paused bench, Pendlay rows for cable rows, barbell extensions for EZ-bar/dumbbells, weighted chins for bodyweight chins, and weighted planks for crunches, and would prefer 3 shorter sessions per week. Overall he calls it a good program that builds a base.

claims.claim: He likes AlphaDestiny and considers him knowledgeable and a good example for natural lifters; the review covers programming only.
Programming videos longer than about 20 minutes are hard to follow, so he splits reviews into parts.

The program defines a novice as someone who can't bench 225, squat 315 and deadlift 405 for 5; he dislikes such strength-based guidelines, especially for a non-powerlifting program, though any healthy male should eventually reach them (not necessarily in year one).
Box squats are a poor choice for novices: not the same motion, stance or muscles as a squat, more lumbar and hip-structure load, less quad, and more technical than people think.
Novices should do free squats; they needn't go ass-to-grass, parallel is fine, and if they can't reach parallel they should work towards it.
Low-rep work (around 5 reps for up to 6 sets) is very doable for novices when sets are not taken to failure.
Alternative lifts in a slot should work similar muscles in similar patterns; floor press and paused bench do not.
Novices should paused bench rather than floor press; floor press depends heavily on arm length and is an accessory for experienced lifters to bring up the bench.
He dislikes Pendlay rows for novices: they lack the mobility and discipline to do them right, cheat with legs and torso, and can hurt their lower back. Cable rows are a safer horizontal pull.
Overhead and behind-the-neck extensions are very important for arm development, but a straight barbell demands elbow and wrist mobility novices lack; use an EZ bar or dumbbells.
Barbell and dumbbell preacher curls are not interchangeable: different strength curve and shoulder stress. Curls are very important for arm development.
3 sets of 6-10 reps is a great rep range for isolation movements.
Good mornings and stiff-leg deadlifts should always be done in higher rep ranges, like 6-10.
Write sets and reps consistently in a program; inconsistent notation confuses readers.

The program's evolving scheme (3-5 sets of 4-6 reps at the same weight) is very intelligent: novices learn to manipulate sets and reps, which prevents plateaus and prepares them for the higher-volume and higher-intensity phases they will need as intermediates. Most novice programs lack this.

Pausing the overhead press is unnecessary for novices; using momentum on the OHP is fine. The real danger is leaning back and turning it into an incline press. Paused OHP is a later tool to bring up touch-and-go OHP.
He dislikes the trap bar, but concedes novices who don't care about the conventional deadlift can use it.
Novices need a lot of horizontal pressing, and the close-grip bench press is a safe way to get it.
Novices should do bodyweight chin-ups/pull-ups until they can consistently hit a clean set of 15 before adding weight, otherwise form and ROM suffer. Most people can't do one pull-up when they start.

For ab size you need a dynamic movement; he prefers crunches over weighted planks, which are also awkward to load without help. Crunches on an incline bench with feet hooked, stretching the abs, are amazing.
Novices should pull from the floor more than once a week, so keep stiff-leg deadlifts.
Two days a week with this much exercise selection means long, high-volume sessions; novices should be babied, and he'd rather they train 3 times a week for an hour than 2 sessions of 2 hours.
Training 3 times a week is better for muscle size because each muscle is hit roughly every two days.
Not using supersets wastes time but is better for performance; too many supersets can burn out a novice.
Including isolation movements in a novice program is very good, though it's odd that all of them sit on workout A.
Any program, including his own, can be criticised; a program can be suboptimal yet still extremely beneficial, and this one will give good gains run as written thanks to its smart rep/set scheme.
You are a novice only briefly but an intermediate/advanced lifter for life, so the novice phase should build a base, prevent future injuries and teach good habits rather than chase performance.
